As a monetary policymaker, I’m especially interested in the fact that these
innovations propelled a surge in the U.S. economy’s productivity
growth—
a.

And according to the latest data, employment in the IT sector is still
contracting—
a.

As I said, until very recently we had been living through a less than stellar
expansion.

The bright spot has been consumer spending, especially when it comes to autos
and housing.

and it’s going to take strength in business investment to keep the
expansion on track.

I must admit, we’ve been expecting to see a solid pickup in growth for quite a while,
because of some very positive fundamentals at work in the economy.
A.

The Fed cut short-term interest rates from six and a half percent to one and
three-quarters percent in 2001.

And we brought the rate down to 1 percent with additional cuts in
November 2002 and last June.

And that bodes well for the future, because faster productivity growth
creates business opportunities that stimulate economic growth.

Business investment in equipment and software—and especially the information
processing equipment component—has showed healthy overall gains,
4

Now, there are downside risks. After all, these positive signals haven’t been sustained
long enough to be conclusive.
A.

One of the main risks is that consumers might pull back, and there are a couple of
reasons why they might.

we’ve built up a lot of slack in labor and product markets over the past 21/2 years—
a.

—the unemployment rate has been at or above six percent for the
last six months,
5

So it’s going to take more than a few quarters of reasonably strong growth
to work off that slack.
a.

In fact—it’s going to take more than a few quarters of quite strong
growth to work it off,

Now, you’re used to hearing central bankers like me cheer when we think inflation is
trending lower.
A.

That makes sense when inflation is clearly too high, because it gets us closer to
the Fed’s main goal, which is price stability.
1.

And price stability, of course, just means an environment where people
and firms can make financial decisions without worrying about where
prices are headed.

and more concern about surprises that could push the inflation rate
lower, possibly even leading to deflation.

Suppose prices fall mainly because of a decline in the demand for goods
and services.
a.

That might happen for a number of reasons, such as a drop in
consumer or business confidence.

But, if prices fall mainly because of an increase in supply—say, due to a
surge in productivity—the situation is very different.
a.

Clearly, it’s the falling demand case—with its potential for a weak
economy—that people worry about.

Over the past couple of years, there appears to have been both a fall in
demand and a surge in supply.
a.

As I mentioned earlier, business demand has been weak, though
we’re now seeing a pickup.
(1)

And we’ve also seen a surge in supply, largely because of the
strong productivity performance I mentioned.
(1)

So, to the extent that we do risk moving toward deflation—and I think that
risk is small—we most likely would face the less worrisome case.

Still, the FOMC has made it clear that further declines in inflation would not be desirable.
Why?
A.

And once the funds rate gets to zero, the Fed can’t push it any lower if it
needs to stimulate the economy.
